chunks: "For a regular silicon PN diode it's about 0. 6 to 0. 7 volts at milliamp currents. The reason is the physics of the junction.

The current is exponential in voltage, I equals I S e to the V over V T , and I S is tiny for silicon, around 10 to the -14 amps for a small diode, because it scales with the square of the intrinsic carrier concentration, which depends exponentially on the bandgap.
To get from 10 to the -14 up to a milliamp you need about eleven decades of current, and at 60 millivolts per decade that's roughly 0. 65 volts. So the 0.
7 volts isn't a hard threshold, it's just where the exponential reaches useful currents.
It goes up about 60 millivolts per tenfold increase in current, and down about 2 millivolts per degree as it heats up.
Different diodes have different drops because the barrier is different. Germanium has a smaller bandgap so it's around 0. 2 to 0. 3 volts.
Schottky diodes use a metal–semiconductor barrier that's lower, so 0. 2 to 0. 45 volts. LEDs use wide-bandgap materials, so a red LED is around 2 volts and blue around 3.
Silicon carbide diodes are higher too. And big high-voltage rectifiers end up around 1 volt at rated current because of their series resistance."
